objectives.summary: Microsoft Sentinel runs on top of a Log Analytics workspace: you create (or pick) a workspace, add Sentinel to it, then connect it to the Microsoft Defender portal for unified security operations. The Defender portal uses one primary workspace (which receives Defender XDR incidents/alerts) plus any number of secondary workspaces. Onboarding to the Sentinel data lake is a separate, one-time, tenant-level step that requires the workspace to be connected as primary. Sentinel in the Azure portal is being retired, so new deployments should be planned around the Defender portal.

keyFacts.fact: Enabling Microsoft Sentinel requires Contributor on the subscription that holds the workspace; default workspaces created by Defender for Cloud can't host Sentinel, and a Sentinel workspace can't later be moved to another resource group or subscription.
New customers who hold subscription Owner or User Access Administrator are automatically onboarded to the Defender portal and use Sentinel there only.

The Defender portal supports one primary and unlimited secondary Sentinel workspaces per tenant; the Defender XDR incidents/alerts connector attaches only to the primary, and switching primary moves that connector automatically.

Onboarding a workspace to the Defender portal requires an unconditional Owner assignment at subscription scope (or User Access Administrator plus Sentinel Contributor); with more than one Sentinel workspace you also need at least Security Administrator in Entra ID.

Data lake onboarding is a one-time tenant setup (up to about 60 minutes) started from System > Settings > Microsoft Sentinel > Data lake; the lake lives in the primary workspace's region, and only same-region connected workspaces are attached. Entra Security Administrator or Global Administrator is required.
After March 31, 2027, Sentinel is supported only in the Defender portal; Workspace Manager isn't available there, so use repositories (preview) or multitenant management to distribute content.

objectives.portalPath: Microsoft Defender portal > System > Settings > Microsoft Sentinel > SIEM workspaces (Connect workspace / Set as primary); Data lake > Start setup

lab.title: Create a Sentinel workspace and connect it to the Defender portal
steps: In the Azure portal, search for Microsoft Sentinel and select Create > Create a new workspace; create resource group RG-SOC and workspace LAW-Contoso-SOC in a data-lake-supported region (for example East US 2).
Back on the Microsoft Sentinel page select Create, choose LAW-Contoso-SOC and select Add.
Sign in to https://security.microsoft.com, go to System > Settings > Microsoft Sentinel > SIEM workspaces.
Select LAW-Contoso-SOC > Connect workspace and set it as Primary; read the product-change notice and confirm.

(Optional, if you have Security Administrator) Go to System > Settings > Microsoft Sentinel > Data lake > Start setup, choose the subscription and resource group for billing, then select Set up data lake.
lab.verify: SIEM workspaces shows the workspace as Connected and Primary, and the Microsoft Sentinel node appears in the Defender portal navigation. If you ran data lake setup, the Data lake settings page shows your subscription/resource group once setup completes.

flashcards.front: How many primary Sentinel workspaces can a tenant have in the Defender portal?
flashcards.back: One primary (receives Defender XDR incidents/alerts) and an unlimited number of secondary workspaces.

flashcards.front: Can you move a Sentinel-enabled workspace to another subscription?
flashcards.back: No. Once Sentinel is deployed on a workspace, moving it to another resource group or subscription isn't supported.

flashcards.front: Which region does the Sentinel data lake use?
flashcards.back: The same region as the primary Sentinel workspace; only connected workspaces in that region are attached, and the region can't be changed afterward from the Defender portal.

questions.scenario: Contoso has three Sentinel workspaces: LAW-EU (West Europe), LAW-US (East US 2) and LAW-APAC (Australia East). All three are connected to the Defender portal. Defender XDR incidents should be correlated with Sentinel alerts from LAW-US.
questions.question: What should you do?
options: Enable the Defender XDR connector in all three workspaces
Set LAW-US as the primary workspace
Use Workspace Manager to make LAW-US the parent workspace
Move LAW-US into the same resource group as the Defender XDR tenant
questions.explanation: Defender XDR incidents/alerts flow only to the primary workspace, and alerts from the primary are correlated with XDR data; setting LAW-US as primary moves the connector there automatically. Enabling the connector everywhere is wrong because the XDR incidents connector binds to the primary only. Workspace Manager isn't available in the Defender portal and has no 'parent' concept for XDR correlation. Resource group placement has no effect on which workspace receives XDR incidents.

objectives.summary: Sentinel SIEM access uses Azure RBAC built-in roles (Reader, Responder, Contributor, Playbook Operator, Automation Contributor), ideally assigned at the resource group that holds the workspace. Playbooks are Logic Apps, so creating/editing them needs Logic App Contributor, and the Sentinel service account needs Automation Contributor on the playbook resource group before automation rules can run them. Data lake access is governed by Microsoft Entra ID roles or Defender unified RBAC.

keyFacts.fact: Reader views data, incidents and workbooks; Responder adds incident management; Contributor adds installing/updating solutions and creating/editing resources such as analytics rules.
Playbook Operator lets a user list, view and manually run playbooks; Logic App Contributor is needed to create or edit playbooks.

Microsoft Sentinel Automation Contributor is assigned to the Sentinel service account (not users) on the playbook resource group so automation rules can run playbooks; granting it requires Owner or User Access Administrator.

Microsoft recommends assigning Sentinel roles at the resource group containing the workspace; if you assign at the workspace instead, you must also assign them on the SecurityInsights solution resource.
Creating or deleting workbooks needs Workbook Contributor in addition to a Sentinel role; guest users who assign incidents need Directory Reader plus Responder.
Playbook Operator, Automation Contributor and Workbook Contributor aren't available in Defender unified RBAC and must still be managed in the Azure portal.

lab.title: Assign least-privilege Sentinel roles to an analyst and grant playbook permissions

Assign Microsoft Sentinel Responder to user Analyst1.
Repeat and assign Microsoft Sentinel Playbook Operator to Analyst1 on the resource group that contains the playbooks.

In Microsoft Sentinel select Settings > Settings > Playbook permissions > Configure permissions, mark RG-SOC and select Apply (requires Owner on RG-SOC). This grants the Sentinel service account Microsoft Sentinel Automation Contributor on that resource group.
lab.verify: Sign in as Analyst1: incidents can be assigned and closed, and Run playbook shows the playbook as runnable (no 'Missing permissions' or 'Grant permission' status).

options: Assign the rule author Microsoft Sentinel Contributor on RG-Playbooks
Grant the Microsoft Sentinel service account the Microsoft Sentinel Automation Contributor role on RG-Playbooks

objectives.summary: The Content hub is the central place to discover, install and update packaged Sentinel solutions (data connectors, analytics rules, workbooks, playbooks, parsers) and standalone content. Solutions are delivered through Azure Marketplace and each item shows its support model (Microsoft, partner, community). Installing a solution often just makes a data connector available; you still configure the connector afterward.

keyFacts.fact: Installing, updating or deleting standalone content or solutions in Content hub requires Microsoft Sentinel Contributor at the resource group level.
Solutions that rely on AMA-based CEF, Syslog or custom-log connectors have dependencies; use 'Install with dependencies' so the required connectors are installed too.

Solutions show an Update status when a newer version exists; solutions are updated from Content hub while standalone content updates automatically. Custom content updates are managed from Repositories.
The install wizard ends with 'Download a template for automation', letting you deploy the solution as code.
In an ISOC workspace in the Defender portal, Content hub (preview) installs only the data connectors from a solution; other content types aren't installed during the preview.

objectives.summary: Microsoft-service connectors fall into API-based, diagnostic-settings-based (some managed by Azure Policy) and agent-based types. Azure Activity uses the diagnostic settings pipeline through an Azure Policy assignment; Entra ID sends sign-in, audit and risk logs; Defender for Cloud has a legacy subscription-based connector and a tenant-based connector (preview) that aligns with Defender XDR incident integration. Several of these sources, such as Azure Activity and Defender alerts, are free to ingest.

keyFacts.fact: Diagnostic-settings connectors managed by Azure Policy need Owner on the policy assignment scope; add a remediation task to apply the policy to existing resources, since by default it applies to new resources.
Policy-managed diagnostic connectors show Connected only if data arrived in the past 14 days.

The Entra ID connector needs Sentinel Contributor on the workspace and Security Administrator on the tenant; ingesting sign-in logs requires Entra ID P1 or P2, while other log types work with any Entra license.

The tenant-based Defender for Cloud connector (preview) collects alerts across the whole tenant; if you integrate Defender XDR incidents, connect it and disconnect the subscription-based (legacy) connector to avoid duplicates.
Bi-directional sync on the Defender for Cloud connector closes the original Defender for Cloud alert when the Sentinel incident is closed.
AzureActivity, Office 365 audit logs (OfficeActivity) and Defender product SecurityAlert data are free data sources in Sentinel.

lab.title: Connect Azure Activity via Azure Policy

On Remediation select Create a remediation task, then Review + create > Create.
Generate activity (for example create and delete a resource group) and wait several minutes.

objectives.summary: The Syslog via AMA and CEF via AMA connectors install the Azure Monitor Agent on a Linux machine (the source itself or a dedicated log forwarder) and push a data collection rule (DCR) that selects facilities and minimum severities. Plain syslog lands in the Syslog table and CEF in CommonSecurityLog. A forwarder also needs the installation script, which configures rsyslog/syslog-ng to listen on port 514.

keyFacts.fact: CEF messages land in CommonSecurityLog and Syslog messages in Syslog; AMA supports RFC 3164 and RFC 5424 syslog formats.
Selecting a log level in the portal DCR collects that level and everything more severe (for example LOG_ERR also collects CRIT, ALERT, EMERG); the API lets you filter specific levels.
Using the same facility for Syslog and CEF can duplicate data between Syslog and CommonSecurityLog; separate facilities or add an ingestion-time transformation to filter CEF out of the Syslog stream.
The forwarder installation script configures rsyslog or syslog-ng and opens port 514 (TCP and UDP); AMA 1.28.11+ receives from the daemon on TCP 28330.
Non-Azure forwarders need Azure Arc (Connected Machine agent) installed to appear in the DCR resource list.
AMA-based data connectors need an internet connection from the agent machine; allow outbound port 443 to Microsoft Sentinel.
In the API DCR, the stream is Microsoft-Syslog for syslog and Microsoft-CommonSecurityLog for CEF.

objectives.portalPath: Microsoft Defender portal > Microsoft Sentinel > Configuration > Data connectors > Common Event Format (CEF) via AMA > Open connector page > +Create data collection rule

lab.title: Build a CEF log forwarder
steps: Deploy a small Ubuntu VM (LinuxFwd01) in the same subscription.
Install the Common Event Format solution from Content hub.
Open CEF via AMA > +Create data collection rule; name it DCR-CEF, select LinuxFwd01 on Resources, and on Collect set LOG_LOCAL4 to LOG_INFO (other facilities none).
Create the rule, then SSH to LinuxFwd01 and run the Forwarder_AMA_installer.py command copied from the connector page.
From the VM run: logger -p local4.warn -P 514 -n 127.0.0.1 --rfc3164 -t CEF "0|Contoso|TestFW|1.0|100|Test|5|src=10.0.0.1"
lab.verify: After a few minutes, CommonSecurityLog | where DeviceVendor == "Contoso" returns the test event, and systemctl status azuremonitoragent shows active.

objectives.summary: The Windows Security Events via AMA connector uses a DCR to collect Security/AppLocker events into SecurityEvent, using predefined sets (All, Common, Minimal) or Custom XPath queries. Windows Event Forwarding (WEF) centralizes events on a Windows Event Collector (WEC); the Windows Forwarded Events connector, with AMA on the WEC, writes them to WindowsEvent instead. Many built-in analytics rules query SecurityEvent, so table choice matters.

keyFacts.fact: All = full Security and AppLocker logs (not Application/System); Common = full user audit trail (includes 4624 and 4634); Minimal = breach-indicating events only (includes 4624/4625/4688 but not 4634); Custom = XPath in the DCR.
Windows Security Events via AMA writes to SecurityEvent; Windows Forwarded Events writes to WindowsEvent, even for forwarded Security log events.
The Windows Forwarded Events connector requires WEC enabled and running with AMA installed on the WEC machine; Microsoft recommends deploying the ASIM WindowsEvent parsers.
AMA supports XPath 1.0 only; test a query with Get-WinEvent -FilterXPath before using it in a DCR.
Non-Azure Windows servers must have Azure Arc installed and enabled before you enable an AMA-based connector.
Selecting the Security log in a generic Azure Monitor DCR sends events to the Event table, whereas the Sentinel connector sends the same events to SecurityEvent.

objectives.portalPath: Microsoft Defender portal > Microsoft Sentinel > Configuration > Data connectors > Windows Security Events via AMA > Open connector page > +Create data collection rule

lab.title: Collect only failed logons with a custom XPath DCR
steps: Install the Windows Security Events solution from Content hub.
On a test Windows VM run in PowerShell: Get-WinEvent -LogName 'Security' -FilterXPath '*[System[(EventID=4625)]]' -MaxEvents 5 to validate the XPath.
Open Windows Security Events via AMA > +Create data collection rule; name DCR-FailedLogon, select the VM on Resources.
On Collect choose Custom and add Security!*[System[(EventID=4625)]], then Review + create > Create.
Generate a failed logon (for example runas /user:fakeuser cmd with a wrong password).
lab.verify: SecurityEvent | where EventID == 4625 returns the new event and no other event IDs arrive from that VM.

objectives.summary: Custom tables store data that has no built-in table. Their names end in _CL and they are fed through DCRs: either text-file collection with AMA (Custom Logs via AMA) or the Logs Ingestion API, where an app sends JSON to a DCR endpoint or DCE. The DCR declares the input stream and an optional KQL transformation that shapes the data to the table schema.

keyFacts.fact: Custom tables used with the Logs Ingestion API must have the _CL suffix; the portal adds it automatically when you create a 'New custom log (DCR-based)'.
The Logs Ingestion API needs an app registration (or managed identity), the target table, a DCR, and the Monitoring Metrics Publisher role on the DCR for the sending identity.
Role assignments on a DCR can take up to 30 minutes to propagate; sending earlier returns HTTP 403.
A Direct-kind DCR provides its own logsIngestion endpoint, so a separate DCE isn't required unless you use private link.
For Custom Logs via AMA, the destination _CL table should contain TimeGenerated (datetime) and RawData (string), or Message when collecting from a forwarder.
Custom columns added to an Azure (built-in) table must use the _CF suffix; certain names such as TenantId, Type and _ResourceId are reserved.

objectives.portalPath: Azure portal > Log Analytics workspaces > (workspace) > Tables > Create > New custom log (DCR-based)

lab.title: Create a custom table and DCR with the Azure CLI
steps: In Cloud Shell (Bash) run: az monitor log-analytics workspace table create --resource-group RG-SOC --workspace-name LAW-Contoso-SOC --name AppAudit_CL --plan Analytics --columns TimeGenerated=datetime RawData=string
Create a DCR JSON (my-dcr.json) with a streamDeclarations entry Custom-AppAudit_CL, a logAnalytics destination for the workspace, and a dataFlow to Custom-AppAudit_CL with transformKql 'source'.
Run: az extension add --name monitor-control-service, then az monitor data-collection rule create --resource-group RG-SOC --name DCR-AppAudit --rule-file ./my-dcr.json
Register an app in Entra ID and assign it Monitoring Metrics Publisher on DCR-AppAudit (Access control (IAM)).
lab.verify: Tables blade lists AppAudit_CL; after sending a sample record with the Logs Ingestion API (or the tutorial PowerShell script) and waiting for propagation, AppAudit_CL | take 10 returns rows.

objectives.summary: Automation rules are lightweight, centrally managed rules triggered when an incident is created or updated or an alert is created; they can assign owners, change status/severity, add tags or tasks, and run playbooks, in a defined order. Playbooks are Azure Logic Apps workflows for complex or external actions (for example, isolating a device or creating a ticket). Calling playbooks directly from analytics rules is deprecated, so automation rules are the way to trigger them.

keyFacts.fact: Automation rule triggers are incident created, incident updated, and alert created; for the alert trigger, the only available action is Run playbook.
Only incident-trigger playbooks can run from incident-trigger rules and only alert-trigger playbooks from alert-trigger rules; both Standard and Consumption logic apps are supported.
Rules run sequentially by Order number and actions run in listed order; later rules see the incident as changed by earlier ones, and update-trigger rules have their own queue.
Rules can have an expiration date, useful for suppressing noise during a time-boxed penetration test.

Adding playbooks directly to analytics rules has been blocked since June 2023, and that legacy method was deprecated as of March 2026; invoke playbooks from automation rules (alert-created trigger) instead.
Changes made by automation rules can be audited with SecurityIncident | where ModifiedBy contains "Automation".

objectives.portalPath: Microsoft Defender portal > Microsoft Sentinel > Configuration > Automation > Create > Automation rule

lab.title: Auto-close pen-test noise with an expiring automation rule
steps: Open Microsoft Sentinel > Configuration > Automation > Create > Automation rule; name it AR-PenTest-Close.
Trigger: When incident is created. Condition: Analytic rule name contains the scheduled rule your pen-test triggers (or tag/IP condition).
Actions: Change status > Closed, classification Benign Positive, comment 'Approved pen test'.
Set Rule expiration to the end of the test window and give it Order 1; select Apply.
lab.verify: Trigger the rule's detection; the new incident is closed automatically, and SecurityIncident | where ModifiedBy contains "Automation" shows the change.

Create a ServiceNow ticket for each new incident

questions.explanation: Assigning owners is a native automation rule action, so a playbook or analytics rule change is unnecessary. External systems need a Logic Apps playbook, triggered by an automation rule; a workbook only visualizes. Automation rules support expiration dates; a playbook timer is more complex, and disabling the analytics rule would lose detections.

questions.scenario: Rule A (Order 1) lowers severity from Medium to Low for incidents from a lab subnet. Rule B (Order 2) runs a paging playbook on incidents with Medium or higher severity. Both use the incident-created trigger.
questions.question: A Medium incident from the lab subnet is created. What happens?
options: Both rules run and the playbook pages the on-call analyst
Rule A runs; Rule B doesn't run because it evaluates the incident after Rule A changed it
Rule B runs first because playbook actions take priority
Neither runs because two rules can't share a trigger
questions.explanation: Rules run in Order sequence and later rules evaluate the incident's state after earlier rules act; after Rule A sets Low, Rule B's Medium-or-higher condition is false. Playbook actions don't jump the queue, and multiple rules can share a trigger.

objectives.summary: Retention in Sentinel combines the Analytics tier (hot, interactive 'analytics retention') with total retention mirrored into the Sentinel data lake for up to 12 years, or ingesting directly to the Data Lake tier for cheap, lower-performance storage. In Azure Monitor terms, tables use the Analytics, Basic or Auxiliary/Lake plan, and long-term retention extends data beyond the interactive window. Settings are per table and managed in the Defender portal Tables page or the Log Analytics Tables blade.

keyFacts.fact: Analytics retention for Sentinel workspaces defaults to 90 days and can be extended to two years (730 days) at a prorated long-term retention charge; total retention can reach 12 years.
Defender XDR advanced hunting data stays in the XDR default tier for 30 days; extending supported XDR tables up to 90 days incurs Sentinel ingestion but no extra storage cost.

Data Lake tier: minimal ingestion cost and slower queries; analytics rules, hunting queries, watchlists, workbooks and playbooks are limited, and Restore and data export aren't available (KQL/notebook jobs can promote data to the analytics tier).
Switching a table from Analytics to Data Lake stops real-time analytics and hunting queries on it; shortening total retention waits 30 days before deleting data.

Basic tables are queryable for 30 days (queries billed per GB scanned); Auxiliary tables are queryable for the whole retention period with unoptimized performance; switching to Auxiliary stops alerts on that table.
A table's plan can be changed only once per week; total retention up to 4,383 days (12 years) can be set per table.

objectives.portalPath: Microsoft Defender portal > Microsoft Sentinel > Configuration > Tables > (table) > Manage table

lab.title: Set analytics and total retention on a table
steps: In the Defender portal open Microsoft Sentinel > Configuration > Tables and select CommonSecurityLog (or another table you ingest).
Select Manage table; set Analytics retention to 180 days and Total retention to 2 years; Save.
Alternatively in the Azure portal: Log Analytics workspace > Tables > ... > Manage table > Data retention settings.
Review Table insights on the Tables page for ingestion volume before choosing Data Lake tier for verbose sources.
lab.verify: The table details pane shows 180 days analytics retention and 2 years total retention.

objectives.summary: Microsoft Purview Audit (the unified audit log) records user and admin activity across Microsoft 365. In the Defender portal you can run the same audit search as in Purview (Audit page), and hunt over Microsoft 365 audit events with KQL in advanced hunting through the CloudAppEvents table, which Defender for Cloud Apps populates when the Microsoft 365 app connector is enabled with Microsoft 365 activities. Purview DLP and insider risk data also surface in advanced hunting tables such as CloudAppEvents and DataSecurityEvents (preview).

keyFacts.fact: CloudAppEvents holds events for accounts and objects in Office 365 and other connected cloud apps; it's populated only if Defender for Cloud Apps is connected to Microsoft 365 with 'Microsoft 365 activities' selected.
To monitor Microsoft 365 activities in Defender for Cloud Apps, auditing must be enabled in Microsoft Purview.
The Defender portal Audit page (security.microsoft.com/auditlogsearch) provides the Purview audit search; access needs the View-Only Audit Logs or Audit Logs role.

Audit (Standard) keeps records 180 days (90 days for logs before Oct 17, 2023); Audit (Premium) keeps Entra, Exchange, OneDrive and SharePoint records one year by default, with retention policies up to 10 years with an add-on.
Advanced hunting explores up to 30 days of raw Defender XDR data, plus analytics-tier data per workspace retention when Sentinel is onboarded.
DLP 'Go hunt' built-in queries (preview) use CloudAppEvents, which contains Purview DLP audit data across SharePoint, OneDrive, Exchange and devices.

objectives.portalPath: Microsoft Defender portal > Investigation & response > Hunting > Advanced hunting (CloudAppEvents); Microsoft Defender portal > Audit

lab.title: Hunt Microsoft 365 file downloads in CloudAppEvents
steps: Confirm auditing is on: in Exchange Online PowerShell run Get-AdminAuditLogConfig | Format-List UnifiedAuditLogIngestionEnabled and expect True. Don't use Security & Compliance PowerShell for this check; there the value always shows False (see https://learn.microsoft.com/purview/audit-log-enable-disable).
In the Defender portal open Settings > Cloud apps > App connectors > Connect an app > Microsoft 365, keep all components (including Microsoft 365 activities) selected and connect.
Download a file from a SharePoint site as a test user.
In Hunting > Advanced hunting run: CloudAppEvents | where ActionType == "FileDownloaded" | project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, Application, ObjectName, IPAddress | take 50
lab.verify: The query returns the test download; the same activity also appears in an Audit search on the Defender portal Audit page.
